record.original_question: Does there exist an infinite family of semigroup conjugacy relations that are first-order definable, that agree with ordinary group conjugacy on every group, and that form a strict chain under inclusion?

evidence.quote: Problem 6.21 from [3] asks whether there exists an infinite set of first-order definable conjugacies that forms: (1) a chain ordered by inclusion or (2) an anti-chain ordered by inclusion.
Thus, {∼n[k]}k∈N is an infinite chain of conjugacies.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A semigroup conjugacy is a binary relation $\sim$ defined uniformly on every semigroup $S$ such that:
(i) on every group, $\sim$ coincides with the ordinary conjugacy relation $a \sim b \iff \exists g\, (b = g^{-1}ag)$; and
(ii) $\sim$ is first-order definable, in the sense that there exists a fixed first-order formula $\varphi(x,y)$ in the language of semigroups $\{\cdot\}$ such that for every semigroup $S$ and every $a,b \in S$, $a \sim b$ if and only if $S \models \varphi(a,b)$.

Question: Does there exist an infinite family $\{\sim_i\}_{i \in I}$ of first-order definable semigroup conjugacies (each satisfying (i) and (ii)) such that the family forms a strictly increasing chain under set-theoretic inclusion of relations? That is, can one find first-order definable semigroup conjugacies $\sim_1, \sim_2, \sim_3, \ldots$ with $\sim_1 \subsetneq \sim_2 \subsetneq \sim_3 \subsetneq \cdots$ when viewed as subsets of $S \times S$ for some witnessing semigroup $S$ (and more generally, forming a strict chain in the inclusion order)?
artifact.status_search_result: The abstract of the source work states explicitly that an infinite chain of first-order definable semigroup conjugacies is constructed, and the extracted text exhibits a family $\{\sim_{n[k]}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ as such a chain, resolving the chain part of the question affirmatively.

status_evidence.claim: The chain version of the problem is resolved affirmatively.
